passage: I was visiting the flat downstairs when the family lit the evening diya. Nandini, who is about two, stopped mid-crawl and stared at the flickering flame. The incense smoke curled up and she followed it with her eyes. Her mouth stayed open. When the chanting began she sat very still with one finger raised, not touching. Her mother let her watch and only guided her hand back. I cannot say what Nandini was thinking, but she did not look away until the song ended.

qa.q: What did Nandini do when the chanting began?
qa.a: She sat very still with one finger raised, not touching.

qa.q: What does Nandini's open mouth and steady gaze suggest she feels?
qa.a: It suggests wonder and curiosity about the flame and smoke. The visitor adds that she cannot say for sure what Nandini was thinking.

qa.q: How did Nandini's mother respond well to her curiosity?
qa.a: She let Nandini watch and only guided her hand back from the flame, so the child could look with wonder without being pushed or hurt.

qa.q: How might the visiting neighbour's view differ from Nandini's experience of the evening?
qa.a: The neighbour sees a still toddler and guesses at wonder. Nandini herself may simply be caught by the light, smell and sound, without any of the words a grown-up would use.

grounding: Flickering diya, incense and chanting hold a toddler's gaze with wonder, and caregivers let her watch gently.

passage: Tuesday: at evening aarti Kunal, two, sat in Dadi's lap and rang the tiny bell while she sang. His father Samir watched from the doorway. Friday: at bedtime Dadi whispered the short prayer, and Kunal leaned back against her, eyelids drooping, and hummed along. Sunday: he found the bell himself, carried it to Dadi and climbed into her lap, patting her hand until she began to sing.

qa.q: What did Kunal ring during aarti on Tuesday?
qa.a: He rang the tiny bell while Dadi sang.

qa.q: What does Kunal's behaviour on Sunday suggest he feels about the prayer time?
qa.a: He seems to feel loved and safe with Dadi, because he fetches the bell and climbs into her lap on his own to ask for it.

qa.q: How can the family keep the prayer time a warm memory and not an obligation?
qa.a: They can keep it gentle, with lap, bell and song, and let Kunal join in his own way as he did on Sunday. 🙂

qa.q: How might Samir see these evenings from the doorway?
qa.a: He probably sees his son at ease and his mother happy, with the ritual being passed on through closeness rather than instruction.

grounding: Sitting in a grandmother's lap during aarti and bedtime prayer makes the child feel loved and part of the family.

passage: I took some soup over to the flat next door and found Yamini walking the room with Vaibhav on her hip. He was hot-cheeked and whimpering, and every time she tried to set him on the cot he clutched her kurta and cried. She did not scold him. She gave him sips of water, spoke to him in a low steady voice and rocked him. "If he stays unwell, I will ring the doctor," she told me quietly.

qa.q: What did Yamini give Vaibhav to drink?
qa.a: She gave him sips of water.

qa.q: Why do you think Vaibhav clutched Yamini's kurta whenever she tried to put him down?
qa.a: He feels ill and hurt and wants the comfort of being held. It is a need for closeness, not naughtiness.

qa.q: What would you advise Yamini if Vaibhav's fever keeps going or worries her?
qa.a: Keep comforting him, and call the doctor rather than waiting, as she already plans to do.

qa.q: How might the neighbour's visit look to Yamini after a long day of holding Vaibhav?
qa.a: Yamini is probably tired and glad of some company and food, though the neighbour only saw part of the day and cannot know how worried she really felt.

grounding: A feverish or hurt child wants to be held and will not be put down; comfort, water and a steady voice are right, and a doctor if it worries.

passage: In the clinic waiting room, Salma, two, clung to her mother's dupatta and stared at the white coat and the tall couch. Dr. Elizabeth smiled and stayed a step back. Salma's mother lifted her onto her lap. "There will be a small pinch, and then it is done. I am right here." When the needle touched, Salma cried and pulled away. Her mother held her close and hummed. Afterwards the doctor gave her a sticker, and Salma slowly stopped sobbing.

qa.q: Who lifted Salma onto her lap before the injection?
qa.a: Salma's mother lifted her onto her lap.

qa.q: What made Salma cry and pull away at the clinic?
qa.a: The white coat, the strange room and the needle frightened her. She could not know what was coming or why.

qa.q: What did Salma's mother do that helped, and what should she avoid?
qa.a: She stayed close, held Salma, and told her the truth simply, that there would be a small pinch. She should never threaten the doctor as a punishment. 🤍

qa.q: How might Dr. Elizabeth see a crying toddler in the clinic?
qa.a: The doctor probably sees fear as normal and stays a step back, smiling. Giving a sticker afterwards shows they want Salma to leave feeling safe.

grounding: White coats and injections frighten a toddler; parents stay close, hold her and tell the simple truth about a small pinch.

passage: Yuki, two, tripped on the pavement outside the bakery and scraped her knee. She sat down hard and her face crumpled. Olga hurried over and crouched. "Ouch. That hurt, didn't it? Your knee is sore." She kissed the scrape lightly and hugged Yuki until the wailing softened to sniffles. Then they looked at the little red mark together. After a minute Yuki wiggled down, tried a careful step, and held her mother's finger.

qa.q: Where did Yuki trip?
qa.a: She tripped on the pavement outside the bakery.

qa.q: What was Yuki feeling when her face crumpled after the fall?
qa.a: She was hurt and probably startled, and she needed to know someone had noticed.

qa.q: Why did Olga name the hurt before doing anything else?
qa.a: Saying "That hurt, didn't it?" tells Yuki her pain matters and is not "nothing". This builds trust and later helps her cope with small falls. 😊

qa.q: What might Yuki take from Olga's response when she meets a fall again?
qa.a: She learns that a grown-up will listen and help, so she can steady herself and try again, as she did with the careful step.

grounding: A kiss on the scrape and a hug after a fall tell the child her pain matters; the hurt is acknowledged, not dismissed.

passage: Note from Ramesh, who minds Jatin at home on weekday afternoons. Tuesday: Jatin's parents began shouting in the next room. Jatin froze with his hands over his ears, then started to cry and grabbed my sleeve. I kept my voice low and lifted him to the back room, away from the noise, and sang a slow song. His body stayed stiff for a while, then softened. I told his mother and father what I saw, and they said they would talk somewhere he cannot hear and reassure him afterwards.

qa.q: Where did Ramesh take Jatin when the shouting began?
qa.a: Ramesh lifted him to the back room, away from the noise.

qa.q: What was Jatin feeling when he covered his ears and grabbed Ramesh's sleeve?
qa.a: He was frightened by a danger he could not understand, and he was looking for someone safe to hold on to.

qa.q: What did the adults agree to do so Jatin is less frightened next time?
qa.a: They said they would talk somewhere he cannot hear and reassure him afterwards. Lowering their voices would help as well.

qa.q: How might Jatin's parents feel when Ramesh tells them what happened?
qa.a: They may feel embarrassed or worried to hear how it looked to a small child. Being told calmly gives them a chance to change, not just feel blamed.

grounding: When adults shout, a toddler freezes, covers her ears and clings; adults move the quarrel away and reassure afterwards.

passage: Monday: Nazia snapped and shouted when the milk spilled. Shreya, two, flinched, hid her face in the cushion and wailed. Tuesday: Shreya sat very quietly and whispered, "Shreya bad." Nazia knelt down. "I shouted. That was not because you are bad. I am sorry." She held her, calm and slow, until Shreya's shoulders dropped. Weeks later, Nazia told the nurse she was shouting too often, and the nurse suggested speaking to a counsellor.

qa.q: What did Shreya whisper on Tuesday?
qa.a: She whispered, "Shreya bad."

qa.q: Why might Shreya think she is bad after the shouting?
qa.a: She is too young to see that it was the adult's stress, so she feels the anger must be her own fault.

qa.q: What did Nazia do to repair things, and what else did she do about the shouting?
qa.a: She knelt, said the shouting was not because Shreya is bad, apologised and held her calmly. Later she told the nurse she was shouting too often and got a suggestion to see a counsellor.

qa.q: How might Nazia have felt telling the nurse about her shouting?
qa.a: She may have felt ashamed or worried, but also wanted to protect Shreya. Asking for help suggests she cares about her daughter. 🤍

grounding: Being shouted at overwhelms a toddler who may blame herself; the caregiver repairs with a calm hug and seeks help if anger at home is frequent.

passage: Note from Vinita, playgroup teacher. At pick-up today I saw Rafiq's mother tell him no more juice. Rafiq dropped to the floor, screamed and kicked his heels. She did not raise her voice. She crouched beside him: "You are so angry. You wanted more juice. No more today." She waited. When his crying eased, she offered water or the picture book. He took the book and sniffled. I shared with her how steady this looked from where I stood.

qa.q: What did Rafiq's mother offer when his crying eased?
qa.a: She offered water or the picture book.

qa.q: What was Rafiq feeling when he dropped to the floor and kicked?
qa.a: He was full of rage and disappointment. He has no words for it yet, so it came out through his body.

qa.q: How did Rafiq's mother hold the limit while helping him?
qa.a: She kept her voice calm, named the feeling, waited out the storm and stayed firm that there was no more juice, while offering a safe alternative.

qa.q: How might Vinita's comment feel to Rafiq's mother after a public tantrum?
qa.a: It may come as relief to hear that someone saw her steadiness and not only the scene. That encouragement helps her repeat the same approach.

grounding: Told no, the toddler screams and drops to the floor; the parent holds the limit, names the feeling and offers an alternative.

passage: Tuesday: at the park gate Pema, two, screamed when Varun said it was time to go. Two weeks later, Pema's mother and grandmother said the same short no to the biscuit tin, and Varun said it too. Later, at the shop, Pema reached for the toffees. "Not today," said Varun. She sighed, dropped her hand and went to pat the shop dog. "Thank you for listening, Pema," he said quietly. The next morning she cried at the gate again, and he stayed calm.

qa.q: Where did Pema scream when Varun said it was time to go?
qa.a: She screamed at the park gate.

qa.q: What did Pema's sigh at the shop show about how she took the no?
qa.a: It showed she had accepted the no this time. She felt a little disappointed but let it go and moved on to the dog.

qa.q: Why did Varun stay calm when Pema cried at the gate again the next morning?
qa.a: Acceptance does not come every time, so he expected it. He kept the limit steady and did not treat her tears as a failure.

qa.q: How does it help Pema that her mother, grandmother and Varun all give the same short no?
qa.a: She hears one clear rule from everyone, so there is nothing to test or bargain over. That makes it easier for her to accept.

grounding: After many calm, consistent limits the toddler sometimes hears no, sighs and moves on, and is quietly praised without expecting it every time.

passage: Sumit's face went hot and his fists tightened. "MINE!" he shouted at Urmila, who was holding the red truck. He grabbed at it once, then stopped when the teacher knelt beside him. "Breathe in with me. Now tell her: 'I am angry, I want it back.'" Sumit took a big breath and said it, his voice shaky. Urmila looked at the truck, then held it out. "Can I have it after you?" Sumit thought. "Okay. After me." 😊

qa.q: What colour was the truck Urmila was holding?
qa.a: The truck Urmila was holding was red.

qa.q: What was Sumit feeling when he shouted "MINE!" and tightened his fists?
qa.a: He was very angry and afraid of losing the truck, and his hot face and tight fists showed how strong the feeling was.

qa.q: What helped Sumit stop grabbing and say what he wanted?
qa.a: The teacher knelt beside him, had him breathe in, and gave him words: "I am angry, I want it back." Naming the feeling let him ask instead of snatch.

qa.q: How might Urmila see Sumit's shout and his later words?
qa.a: The shout probably felt scary or unfair to her. When he used words, she could hand the truck back and ask for a turn afterwards.

grounding: A child with hot face and tight fists shouts 'MINE!' and a grown-up helps him say he is angry and wants the toy back.
